steps.body:
In C1 you learned that **f′ = 0 is a suspect, not a conviction**. This course is where the suspects get tried.

A **critical point** is any x where f′(x) = 0 **or f′ does not exist**. Those are the only places an interior extremum can hide — everywhere else the curve is visibly climbing or falling, and a climbing curve is not at a peak.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x². Drag x to the one place where the tangent is flat — the only critical point this curve has.
widget.successFeedback: x = 0, where f′ = 0. And read the curve you drew underneath: f′ = 2x crosses zero there, going from negative to positive. The crossing is what makes it a genuine minimum — but that is the next lesson. For now: a flat tangent marks a place worth investigating.
widget.lowFeedback: The tangent is still tipping downhill (f′ < 0). Keep sliding right.
widget.highFeedback: The tangent is tipping uphill now (f′ > 0). You have gone past the flat spot.

predict.prompt: On y = x², you need the tangent slope to read 0. Starting from x = -3, you'll find it…

options.label: To the right of where you start
To the left of where you start
In two places — either direction works

predict.reveal: On x² the slope at x is 2x — it climbs steadily left to right, so slope 0 lives at exactly one spot: x = 0. One slope, one place; that's what makes 2x a function of x.

cml.actionGoal: Move along a function and coordinate position, local slope, and derivative graph.

explanationVariants: f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x² = 4, so x = ±2. Two critical points.
Setting the derivative to zero is how critical points are FOUND. Deciding what they ARE is a separate question.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ − 12x. How many critical points does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x² = 4, and a square equals 4 at TWO values: x = 2 and x = −2.
The derivative does hit zero: 3x² = 12 at x = ±2.
A quadratic derivative has at most two roots, and here it has exactly two.

explanationVariants: |x| has no derivative at 0 — the corner. That is still a critical point, and in fact it is a minimum, even though f′ never equals zero anywhere.
Defining critical points as 'f′ = 0' alone would miss every corner and cusp, and would miss the minimum of |x| entirely.

widget.prompt: Why does the definition include 'f′ does not exist' as well as 'f′ = 0'?

options.label: Because |x| has a minimum at its corner, where f′ does not exist at all.
options.feedback: Right — a definition that said only 'f′ = 0' would miss that minimum entirely. Extrema can hide at corners.

options.label: For completeness; it never actually happens.
options.feedback: It happens constantly — every corner, cusp and vertical tangent. And |x| puts a genuine minimum at one.

options.label: Because f′ = 0 is hard to solve.
options.feedback: Difficulty is not the reason. The reason is that some extrema sit at points where no tangent exists.

options.label: Because a vertical tangent is a maximum.
options.feedback: A vertical tangent might be a maximum, a minimum, or neither — which is exactly why it must be treated as a SUSPECT rather than ignored.

steps.body:
So the procedure has two halves, and the second is the hard one:

**Find** the critical points: solve f′ = 0, and find where f′ is undefined.
**Classify** them: peak, valley, or neither.

Finding is algebra. Classifying is calculus — and it is where the rest of this chapter lives.
A critical point that is neither.
explanationVariants: f′(x) = 3x² is zero at x = 0, but it is positive on both sides — so f climbs into the point and climbs out. No extremum.
This is the x³ trap from C1, and it is the reason 'find' and 'classify' must be separate steps.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x³ has a critical point at x = 0. What is it?

options.label: Neither a peak nor a valley — f′ = 3x² is positive on BOTH sides, so f keeps climbing.
options.feedback: Right. Finding a critical point proves nothing on its own. This is the whole reason the classification step exists.

options.label: A minimum.
options.feedback: A minimum needs the curve to FALL into it and rise out. Here it rises in and rises out — it merely pauses.

options.label: A maximum.
options.feedback: The curve is higher just to the right of 0 than at 0, so it cannot be a maximum.

options.label: Impossible to tell.
options.feedback: You can tell, and easily: f′ = 3x² is positive either side, so f is climbing on both sides. That settles it.

hints: Differentiate first, then factor. Do not expand needlessly.
That is zero when x² = 0 or x = 3. Count the DISTINCT solutions.
explanationVariants: f′ = 4x²(x − 3) is zero at x = 0 and x = 3: two critical points. (The x = 0 root is doubled, which will matter enormously in the next lesson.)
A repeated root of f′ is a critical point where f′ touches zero without crossing — remember that phrase.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x⁴ − 4x³. How many DISTINCT critical points does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: The factor x² gives a repeated root at 0, but it is still only ONE point. Distinct solutions: x = 0 and x = 3.
4x²(x − 3) = 0 has two distinct solutions: x = 0 and x = 3.
The derivative certainly reaches zero — at x = 0 and x = 3.

widget.fallbackFeedback: f′ = 4x²(x − 3) = 0 → x = 0 (doubled) and x = 3: two distinct critical points.

takeaways: A critical point is where f′ = 0 OR f′ does not exist. Both kinds can hide an extremum.
Finding them is algebra; classifying them is calculus, and they are separate steps.
x³ has a critical point that is neither a peak nor a valley. The suspect was innocent.
steps.teaser: Next: the trial. What f′ does on EITHER SIDE decides the verdict.

concept.body: Differentiate. Set it to zero. Solve. Then also ask: is there anywhere f′ fails to exist — a corner, a cusp, a vertical tangent? Every such x is a suspect, and no other x is.

explanationVariants: One linear derivative, one critical point.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x² − 6x + 1. Find its critical point.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the coefficient. Set f′ = 2x − 6 to zero: x = 3.
That is the constant term, which differentiates away entirely.
